summary:
Alabama stands under the United States national framework, which applies in every state. Travel documents are the sharpest exposure: since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction at state level. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a visitor encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Alabama's own facility bans, enacted in 2022 and 2024, are in force. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update records that Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing the state in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-eroding jurisdictions. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates these state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Internal risk assessments are equally stark. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Recorded killings of trans women in Alabama stand at 3.8 per 100,000 per year, an undercount floor, on the 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025, according to The Needle's July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams data. That analysis grades Alabama in the worst-law group.
tangentialFactors:
Alabama's placement in the worst-law grouping is a pattern finding, not an isolated one: the July 2026 assessment applies the same grading across jurisdictions, and four states are separately designated do-not-travel for trans people, with Idaho the most recent addition on 13 July 2026.

The direction of travel is consistent across layers. Federal measures on documents and visas, a 2026 legislative season described as continuing to degrade trans rights, and state facility bans enacted in 2022 and 2024 all move the same way, which means a visitor's exposure is cumulative rather than confined to a single rule.

Facility restriction is a majority-of-states phenomenon in practice: bans are in force in nine states and one territory, with further states imposing outright bans on gender-identity-based facility use, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have none. Alabama sits on the restricting side of that divide.

Comparable jurisdictions show that document rules vary sharply at state level. Kansas has invalidated birth certificates and licences not bearing sex assigned at birth and barred trans residents from changing those markers, and rights groups describe it as a template; a visitor's document position therefore changes at state lines even while federal passport rules apply everywhere.

Foreign governments treat the United States as a heightened-risk destination for trans travellers. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted their travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Alabama itself carries a do-not-travel designation is unresolved in the sources: the 13 July 2026 assessment names Idaho as the latest of four states so flagged, and Alabama is not identified as one of the four, though it is graded in the worst-law group on other criteria.

The status of Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' bill as cited by the July 2026 assessment is not resolved in the inventory: the source describes it as carrying a bathroom ban extending to college campuses but does not state whether the provision is enacted, enjoined, or under litigation at the time of writing.

No Alabama-specific enforcement incidents are sourced. The only documented arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law in the inventory occurred in April 2025 at the Florida state capitol, and it is not established here whether Alabama authorities have made comparable arrests or brought prosecutions under the 2022 and 2024 bans.

The 3.8 per 100,000 figure is explicitly an undercount floor derived from a 428-victim national base for 2008 to 2025; the sources do not provide a year-by-year Alabama series, a confidence interval, or a comparison against other states' rates.

Whether Alabama's state-issued identification documents permit gender-marker changes, and under what conditions, is not stated in this inventory; the Movement Advancement Project map is cited as the reference that sets this out state by state but its Alabama entry is not reproduced here.
